To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) positive data and negative information provided by the teacher can be used to compensate for full data, but (2) this can be done only if the negative information is provided in a timely manner, and (3) the teacher can provide the learner with the least negative counterexamples.

(1) for Gold's model, negative counterexamples are as powerful as positive data; (2) for behaviorally correct model, negative counterexample is as powerful as full positive and negative examples; (3) for Gold's and behaviorally correct models, negative counterexamples provided after a finite time can be as powerful as negative counterexamples provided immediately.

negative data can help in the following ways: (1) to reduce the number of errors in a learner; (2) to reduce the time of learning; (3) to reduce the amount of positive data needed; (4) to increase the learning power; (5) to compensate for negative data; (6) to compensate for the lack of positive data; (7) to compensate for both positive and negative data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
learning in the limit from positive data and (potentially negative) counterexamples.
learning in the limit with negative counterexamples and with exploring how negative counterexamples affect learning power of different learning paradigms.
the interplay between the positive data and negative information, and with the role of the latter in language learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
negative counterexamples can be used in learning languages in the positive data model, but they are not necessary, except for behaviorally correct learners.
negative counterexamples can help in learning, but not as much as one might think.
negative data can be very powerful, but they can also be very harmful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of negative counterexamples in a learning process can be a blessing and a curse, depending on the learning model considered.
, for learning languages from positive data, negative counterexamples can be helpful, but they are not always needed.
negative counterexamples provided to a learner can be very helpful, but only if they are obtained immediately and in a certain way.
The main takeaway from our work is that
negative data can be a powerful tool in the hands of a learner.
negative data can be used to learn languages in the limit, and that this is done in different and sometimes surprisingly powerful ways.
negative counterexamples provided to learners by a teacher can have a significant positive impact on the learning power of learners.
